title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
A class-action lawsuit alleges that Otter.ai's transcription service automatically joins virtual meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams without the consent of all participants, records conversations, and uses them to train its AI systems. The suit claims this violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws. The company states it obtains permission through user agreements, though the lawsuit argues that users are deceived about the scope of this use.

The failure here is a mismatch between what a system was designed to do and the context in which it operates. A transcription tool built to record meetings where the user operates it is deployed in an environment where automatic, background joining means third parties have no notice or control. Whether the company's de-identification of data is effective, and whether users genuinely understood what they consented to, are not established by the reporting and remain contested in court.

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a popular AI transcription service, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission and using them to train its systems. The suit alleges that Otter's software automatically joins virtual meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams without obtaining consent from all participants, then shares recordings with the company to improve its artificial intelligence. Plaintiff Justin Brewer claims his privacy was severely violated when he discovered his confidential conversation had been recorded. The lawsuit contends that Otter's practices violate state and federal privacy and wiretap laws and that the company profits financially from this covert activity.

Otter.ai, based in Mountain View, California, has approximately 25 million users and has recorded over one billion meetings since its founding in 2016. The company claims it receives explicit permission through user agreements to use meeting transcripts for training purposes, though the lawsuit argues many users are still being deceived. Recent concerns have emerged from various users, including an AI researcher whose confidential business details were exposed and a journalist interviewing a human rights activist, raising fears about potential government access to sensitive conversations. Otter maintains it de-identifies data before using it in machine learning systems, but the lawsuit questions the effectiveness of this process.
